E072-01.notes: Comma splice in A; B fused; D 'and, it' mispunctuated. Semicolon joins two independent clauses.

E072-02.notes: A, C, D all redundant. Shortest answer is also correct, which is normal for ACT redundancy items.

E072-03.notes: Sentence about adhesives in general is off-topic. A and B misdescribe the sentence; C invents a contradiction.

E072-04.notes: Choir detail sets up the hymnal in sentence 5. D is false because the choir isn't mentioned earlier. B is a plausible trap but the detail supports the main story.

E072-05.notes: Plural subject 'slips' and past-tense narrative ('realized') need 'kept'. B is singular and the wrong tense; D is not a finite verb.

E072-06.notes: The 1977 failure contrasts with the 1978 success. 'As a result' doesn't work because the failure didn't cause the success; B and D are illogical.

E072-07.notes: Register item: A, B and C are all informal; D is neutral and fits the purchase context. Matches the 1978 Boise result (about 90% of people who tried the samples said they would buy).

E072-08.notes: Only B speaks to how widely the product came to be used. C is about variety and D about production.

E072-09.notes: Calls back to the 'useless'/no-practical-use idea in the opening. B, C and D bring in new, unrelated details.

E072-10.notes: A is false (no chemistry in the essay); B mischaracterizes the focus; D is false because the essay mentions the 1977 Press 'n Peel failure.

E072-11.notes: No comma between two items joined by 'and'. C and D are clearly wrong. Facts check out: jeans and a campaign hat in 1944.

E072-12.notes: Sentence 6's 'That spring' needs a year as its antecedent, and only D supplies 1950 and the transition to the real cub. This dependency is a legitimate cue, not a giveaway. The fact is accurate (Capitan Mountains, spring 1950).

E072-13.notes: General bear fact interrupts the narrative. D's 'contradiction' doesn't hold because the passage never says the cub was with its mother; A and B are unsupported.

E072-14.notes: Object of 'named' ('officials named him Smokey'), so 'whom'. C creates a comma splice; D is possessive. Using who/whom for an animal is acceptable for a named individual animal, and 'which' is not offered.

E072-15.notes: 'Until 1976' plus past narrative requires 'lived'. Smokey stayed at the National Zoo until his death in 1976 (he was retired in 1975 but remained at the zoo), so the statement is accurate.

E072-16.notes: The ZIP code (20252, assigned in 1964 because of heavy mail) is concrete evidence of fame. A is vague and redundant; B and C are irrelevant.

E072-17.notes: A, C and D are redundant.

E072-18.notes: The stem asks for the reason for the slogan change; only C gives one. Factually acceptable: the 2001 change reflected that the campaign targets unwanted wildfires (including in grasslands) as distinct from beneficial prescribed fires. Simplified but accurate.

flags.note: Options are listed out of numeric order (A: Sentence 3, B: Sentence 1, C: Sentence 6, D: Sentence 9). ACT placement items list sentences in ascending order; reorder to Sentence 1/3/6/9.

E072-19.notes: 'Its' refers to 'the first poster', which shows the bear pouring water on a campfire. After 9, 'Its' could point to the slogan, but the wildfire slogan's message isn't about campsites, and that placement would split 9 from the reason given in 10/18. Sentence 4 isn't offered, so only one answer works.
